beats.narration_text: Research Computing on Explorer and AICR. Intro to Linux. The shell commands every cluster user needs: moving around, files, permissions, and the habits that keep a shared system happy.

shot.visual_intent: Film identity and short teaching description, visible immediately; Liam speaks playlist, title, summary

beats.narration_text: Salaam. This is Liam, in for Bear. First, a correction. The terminal isn't an old way to use a computer. It's the direct way, and on a cluster it's the main one: the keyboard becomes your only input. This lecture is the basics of the Linux terminal: what Linux is, how to find your way around the file system, how to make, move and remove files, how to read them, who may do what to them, two editors, and three tips that save you every day.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. The kernel: the core of an operating system, the part that talks to the hardware. A shell: the program that reads what you type and runs it. A directory: a folder. A path: the address of a file, written from the root slash or from where you stand. Root: the administrator account that may do anything. And a flag: a dash and a letter that changes what a command does.

beats.narration_text: Linux is a family of operating systems built on the Linux kernel, which Linus Torvalds created in 1991 in the tradition of Unix, the much older system that also shaped macOS. It runs on Android phones, on laptops, and on nearly every HPC cluster. It's free and open source, so anyone can contribute and a huge toolbox comes at no cost, and it's considered secure and robust, which is why servers and clusters run it.

beats.narration_text: Linux has graphical desktops, but underneath is the command line, reached through a terminal. The prompt tells you four things: your user name, the host you're on, where you are, and what kind of user you are. A dollar sign means a normal user. A hash means root, the administrator. A normal user can't install system packages: ask, and you're told you're not in the sudoers file.

beats.narration_text: The file system is files and directories, as on Windows or a Mac. The terminal colours them: blue for directories, green for executables, red for compressed archives, plain for ordinary files. A path is a file's address. Absolute: from the root, starting with a slash. Relative: from where you stand. One dot is here. Two dots is one level up.

beats.narration_text: Three commands move you around. p w d prints where you are; the tilde is your home. l s lists what's here. Flags change it: dash l for the long listing with permissions, owner, size and date; dash a for everything, including hidden files, whose names start with a dot. Flags combine, dash l a.

beats.narration_text: c d changes directory. c d into a folder; the prompt shows you're there. c d dot dot goes one level up. c d alone, or c d tilde, takes you home from anywhere.
beats.motion_claim: The training's own terminal session replays line by line, verbatim.

beats.narration_text: Making things. touch creates an empty file. To put text in one, redirect: a single greater-than overwrites the file, a clean slate; a double one appends to the end. cat shows the result. And make-dir, m k d i r, makes a directory.
beats.motion_claim: The training's own terminal session replays line by line, verbatim.

beats.narration_text: C P copies a file; a directory needs dash capital R, recursive, to copy what's inside. The original stays. m v moves, and moving a file to a new name is how you rename.
beats.motion_claim: The training's own terminal session replays line by line, verbatim.

beats.narration_text: r m removes a file; dash r removes a directory and everything in it. There is no trash can and no undo. On a cluster, a removed file is gone, so read the command twice before you press return.

beats.narration_text: A symbolic link is a shortcut, like an alias on a Mac. l n dash s, then the target, then the name you want: point to target, call it link name. In a long listing it starts with l and shows an arrow to where it points. Now c d my_data jumps to the deep directory. Move or delete the original and the link breaks.
beats.motion_claim: The training's own terminal session replays line by line, verbatim.

beats.narration_text: Reading a file. cat dumps the whole thing into the terminal, fine for a short one. For a long one use less: a scrollable viewer. Arrows move a line, Page Up and Page Down a page, Home and End jump to the ends, and q quits. Escape does not close it.

beats.narration_text: Who may do what. Every file has three audiences: the user who owns it, the group that owns it, and others, everyone else. And three permissions: read, write, and execute, which for a directory means entering it. Each permission has a number: read four, write two, execute one.

shot.visual_intent: A 3×3 grid draws: columns user · group · others (small tokens: one figure, three figures, a crowd), rows read · write · execute with their numerals 4 · 2 · 1 beside; cells fill as spoken; a small directory icon beside 'execute' gets a door. Act title top-left.
shot.motion_claim: A 3×3 grid draws: columns user · group · others (small tokens: one figure, three figures, a crowd), rows read · write · execute with their numerals 4 · 2 · 1 beside; cells fill as spoken; a small directory icon beside 'execute' gets a door. Act title top-left.

beats.narration_text: Here's a real long-listing line, decoded. The first character is the type: dash for a file, d for a directory, l for a link. Then nine characters in three groups of three: the owner's permissions, the group's, everyone else's. r w x: the owner can read, write and execute. r w dash: the group can read and write but not run. r dash dash: others can only read. After that: the link count, the owner, the group, the size in bytes, the modification time, and the name.

shot.visual_intent: The mono line '-rwxrw-r-- 1 user group 46 Feb 14 16:37 File.txt' sits large on the stage; brackets rise under each part as spoken, with small labels (type · owner · group · others · links · owner · group · size · time · name); the three permission triads lift apart and each gets its reading in words.

beats.narration_text: Changing permissions with c h mod. By symbol: who, plus or minus, which. g plus x gives the group execute. u minus x takes it from the owner. Combinations join with commas. Or by number: three digits, owner, group, others, each the sum of four, two and one. Seven five one is read-write-execute for the owner, read and execute for the group, execute only for others.
beats.motion_claim: The training's own terminal session replays line by line, verbatim.

beats.narration_text: And ownership with c h own: user colon group, then the file. Dash capital R for a whole directory.
beats.motion_claim: The training's own terminal session replays line by line, verbatim.

beats.narration_text: Two editors live in the terminal. Nano is the simple one: nano and a file name. Its shortcuts are listed along the bottom, and the caret means Control. Vim is the powerful one, with two modes. In normal mode you can't type into the file. Press i for insert mode and type. Press Escape to get back to normal mode. Type colon w q to save and quit. Stuck? Escape, then colon q exclamation mark quits without saving.

beats.narration_text: Three tips. Tab completes a long name: type the start, press Tab, the shell fills the rest. Control C stops a running program, or throws away a line you've mistyped. And clear wipes the screen.
beats.motion_claim: The training's own terminal session replays line by line, verbatim.

beats.narration_text: That's the terminal. Prompt, path, list, move, make, copy, remove with care, read, permissions, an editor, and Tab. Questions go to the Research Computing team at r c help at northeastern dot e d u, or to office hours on Zoom.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. The prompt shows your user, host, location, and whether you're root. p w d, l s with flags, and c d move you; absolute paths start from the root; a single dot means here, two dots mean up. touch, redirection, make-dir, C P dash R, M V; r m has no undo; l n dash s makes a shortcut. cat for short files, less for long ones, q quits. Read, write, execute for user, group and others, changed with c h mod by symbol or by number. Nano is simple; vim is i, Escape, colon w q. Tab completes, and Control C stops.

artifactLines: The prompt: user, host, where you are, $ or #.
pwd, ls -la, cd; absolute paths start with /, . is here, .. is up.
touch, > and >>, mkdir, cp -R, mv; rm has no undo; ln -s target link.
cat for short files, less for long ones; q quits.
rwx for user, group, others; chmod by symbol or by 4-2-1 numbers.
nano is simple; vim: i, ESC, :wq. Tab completes, Ctrl+C stops.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: I'm new to the Linux terminal on a cluster. Give me a ten-command practice session: make a project folder in my home directory with two subfolders, create a notes file with one line, append a second line, copy it into a subfolder, rename the copy, make the file readable by my group but not by others, and show me the long listing after each step so I can see what changed. Explain each command in one sentence. Then check two things yourself. Did every path it wrote start with a slash or a tilde? And did it warn you before the first r m?
